# ADR-0007: Point references are positions, not identifiers

> **Status:** accepted | **Date:** 2026-07-29

**References:** [ADR-0005](../adr/ADR-0005.md), [RFC-0002:C-APPROX](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-approx), [RFC-0002:C-MEMORY](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-memory), [RFC-0005:C-BINDING](../rfc/RFC-0005.md#rfc-0005c-binding), [RFC-0005:C-IDENTITY](../rfc/RFC-0005.md#rfc-0005c-identity), [RFC-0007:C-BAKE](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-bake), [RFC-0007:C-EDIT](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-edit), [RFC-0007:C-PROVENANCE](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-provenance)

## Context

[RFC-0007:C-EDIT](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-edit) 3 left point identity unspecified, and two things depend on it: enumerated
point-set edits, and the consolidated form of an edit stack ([RFC-0007:C-BAKE](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-bake)). Neither LAS nor
COPC provides a point identifier.

Because region edits were designed specifically to avoid needing identity, this is a much smaller
problem than it first appeared. Identity is off the common path, so it can be internal, cheap, and
narrowly scoped rather than a format-level guarantee.

Both comparable tools were examined and they converge. QGIS 3.42 introduced point cloud editing and
keys it on a position in a container: its undo command stores a map of sub-index to node id to a
per-node record holding point-index-to-prior-value, and the edit itself is constructed from
`QHash<int, QHash<QgsPointCloudNodeId, QVector<int>>>` — sub-index, then node, then indices within
the node. CloudCompare uses the array index of an in-memory cloud, with an explicit
indices-into-another-cloud structure for selections.

More instructive than the representation is that **neither solves reference invalidation; both forbid
the operations that cause it.** QGIS refuses to edit point positions, and refuses to edit anything but
a local COPC — so reprojection is a display transform and the file is never rewritten. CloudCompare
holds a single array, so a rigid transform is applied in place and indices survive, while resampling
yields a separate cloud.

That reframed the question. Reprojection had looked like the hazard, and it is not: [RFC-0007:C-EDIT](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-edit)
5 already makes sources read-only, and reprojection is an output concern rather than a document
mutation, so it cannot orphan a reference. The actual hazard is **graph position**. ADR-0005 chose to
put edits in the document graph partly so an edit could sit between two processing steps — and that is
exactly where identity dies: an enumerated reference taken downstream of a decimation or voxelisation
names operator output, which ceases to exist when that operator's parameters change, an ordinary user
action.

A second hazard has no analogue in either tool, because it is created by the non-destructive design.
QGIS cannot experience it: the file is the state, so edits and data cannot disagree. Here edits live
beside an immutable source, so if a source is replaced at the same location by a reprocessed file,
every node key and index still resolves and now names different points. References would be silently
wrong and [RFC-0007:C-PROVENANCE](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-provenance) would record an audit trail of nonsense.

## Decision

A point reference is a position in a fingerprinted source version, and point-set edits may attach only
directly to a source. The obligations are written in [RFC-0005:C-IDENTITY](../rfc/RFC-0005.md#rfc-0005c-identity) and
[RFC-0005:C-BINDING](../rfc/RFC-0005.md#rfc-0005c-binding); this ADR records only *why*.

Why a **positional reference** rather than a minted or content-derived identifier:

- **It is free.** Node key plus index within node is already how points are addressed in order to read
  them, so identity requires no store, no minting pass, and no ingest rewrite.
- **Minting does not scale to the premise.** A persisted 128-bit identifier per point costs roughly
  sixteen gigabytes per billion points — sidecar storage proportional to a population defined by not
  fitting in memory — to support an escape hatch used twelve points at a time.
- **Content identity is not unique in LiDAR.** Coincident and near-coincident returns are ordinary, so
  a digest of position and attributes collides, and it collides hardest in dense cluttered regions,
  which is precisely where manual correction happens.
- **It is what production tools do.** QGIS keys its edits on sub-index, node id and index within node;
  CloudCompare uses the array index of an in-memory cloud. This is the converged answer, not a
  shortcut.

Why safety comes from **restricting use** rather than from durability, which is the transferable
lesson from both tools — neither migrates references, both forbid what invalidates them:

- **Reprojection was a false alarm.** [RFC-0007:C-EDIT](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-edit) 5 makes sources read-only and reprojection is
  an output concern, so no reference can be orphaned by it. QGIS relies on the same avoidance.
- **Graph position is the real hazard.** A reference taken downstream of a cardinality-changing
  operator names that operator's output, which vanishes when its parameters change — an action a user
  has every reason to take. Confining point-set edits to sources eliminates the class, and costs little
  because the enumerated form is the rare escape hatch while region edits remain placeable anywhere.

Why a **fingerprint**, and why the cheap one:

- **Non-destructive editing creates a hazard the precedents cannot have.** Where the file is the state,
  edits and data cannot disagree. Here they can: a source replaced in place by a reprocessed file still
  resolves every node key and index, silently naming different points.
- **Header and hierarchy, not the whole file, where a hierarchy exists.** Digesting a 500 GB remote COPC
  to decide whether to trust it reads the entire file, contradicting the project's premise about as
  directly as anything could. The header and hierarchy are small, already fetched to traverse the source
  at all, and rewritten by any reprocessing that changes point content. Formats without a hierarchy
  offer nothing cheaper than the file, and are usually indexed on ingest anyway, so the digest rides
  along on a pass already happening.
- **Streaming BLAKE3.** Bounded memory keeps [RFC-0002:C-MEMORY](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-memory) intact even for the whole-file case,
  and the algorithm is named in the clause because persisted fingerprints are a compatibility surface.

Why **read-only** on mismatch rather than refusing to open or marking results approximate: refusing
protects nothing additional while making a recoverable situation feel like data loss; marking results
approximate under [RFC-0002:C-APPROX](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-approx) misdescribes the failure, since "approximate" is the wrong word
for twelve references that now name twelve different points. Read-only preserves every edit, evaluates
nothing against stale references, and reports *which* edits are affected so the user can re-point or
discard them deliberately.

## Consequences

### Positive

Identity costs nothing to implement and nothing to store, so the enumerated escape hatch is affordable.
Source substitution — otherwise a silent corruption that [RFC-0007:C-PROVENANCE](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-provenance) would dutifully record
as fact — becomes a detected condition with named affected edits.

Non-destructive evaluation also keeps undo free of per-point state, and this is worth recording because it
is a property easily traded away. A destructive editor must retain a prior value for every edited point:
QGIS does exactly that, storing point-index-to-prior-value per node. Here evaluation is a pure function of
an immutable source and an ordered edit stack, so undo is removing a node and re-evaluating, with no
per-point memory at all. An implementation that introduced a prior-value store to make undo feel faster
would forfeit this without any obligation appearing to have been broken.

### Negative

Point-set edits cannot be placed mid-pipeline, so the two edit forms have different placement rules that
the interface must make legible rather than leaving as a surprise. Every derived artefact must carry the
fingerprint it was built from. Sources without a spatial index need a full-file digest, which is I/O-bound
on first open.

A byte-level substitution preserving header and hierarchy while altering point records is undetectable
under the cheap digest — named in [RFC-0005:C-BINDING](../rfc/RFC-0005.md#rfc-0005c-binding) rather than hidden, and accepted because detecting
it means fully reading every source on every open.

### Neutral

References do not survive resampling, by design rather than omission — a resample produces points that no
node key and index address, so there is nothing for a reference to survive *to*.

Three drifts to watch. First, pressure to automatically re-resolve stale references by proximity, which is
the one option that produces a wrong forestry number with no signal, and is forbidden by
[RFC-0005:C-IDENTITY](../rfc/RFC-0005.md#rfc-0005c-identity) 2 for that reason. Second, the positional restriction being relaxed "just for this
operator" — every such relaxation reintroduces references to operator output. Third, the point-set form
becoming the default because enumerating selected points is easier to implement than good region tooling.

Reversal cost is low for the decision itself and unchanged for its alternatives. Adding minted identifiers
later is additive, and the positional restriction can be relaxed if a durable reference mechanism ever
justifies it — so nothing here locks the project in. What does not get cheaper is the rejected options: the
sidecar still costs sixteen gigabytes per billion points, and content-derived identity still collides on
coincident returns. Revisiting this means paying the price that was declined, not undoing something.

The one genuinely irreversible element is not part of this decision: the fingerprint algorithm is a field in
saved documents, so changing it is a breaking format change. That is an obligation rather than a
consequence, and it is stated as [RFC-0005:C-BINDING](../rfc/RFC-0005.md#rfc-0005c-binding) 6.

## Alternatives Considered

### Positional composite reference — source, version fingerprint, node key, index within node — with point-set edits restricted to attaching directly to a source (accepted)

- **Pros:** Free: it is already how points are addressed, so no store and no minting, Matches both comparable implementations, so the approach is proven in production, Restricting graph position removes the whole class of operator-output invalidation, The fingerprint makes source substitution detectable rather than silently wrong, Requires no per-point state at all, so undo stays free under non-destructive evaluation
- **Cons:** References do not survive resampling, and are not intended to, Point-set edits cannot be placed mid-pipeline, unlike region edits, A cheap header-and-hierarchy digest cannot detect a byte-level swap that preserves both

### Minted persistent identifiers: assign each point a 128-bit id at ingest and persist it in a sidecar store (rejected)

- **Pros:** Survives resampling, reprojection, rewriting — everything, References remain valid wherever they appear in the graph, with no positional restriction, Would also serve future joins and cross-source provenance
- **Cons:** Roughly sixteen gigabytes of sidecar per billion points, for datasets defined by not fitting in memory, Ingest becomes a mandatory rewriting pass over every source, including remote ones, The sidecar is a second store to keep consistent with a source that may change beneath it
- **Rejected because:** The storage cost scales with the point population, in a project whose premise is that the point population does not fit. Sixteen gigabytes of identifiers to support an escape hatch used for twelve points at a time inverts the cost of the feature and its value, and it would require a full rewriting pass over sources that may be remote and read-only.

### Content-derived identity: digest each point's position and attributes, or quantise its position, and use that as the reference (rejected)

- **Pros:** Needs no sidecar and no minting — identity is a pure function of the point, Survives resampling and file rewriting, since it depends only on content
- **Cons:** Coincident returns are ordinary in LiDAR, so distinct points collide, Collisions land precisely on the points a user is most likely to be correcting, Does not survive reprojection, since coordinates are part of the content
- **Rejected because:** Coincident and near-coincident returns are normal in LiDAR, so content identity is not unique in practice — and the collisions concentrate on dense, cluttered regions, which is exactly where manual correction happens. An identity scheme that is least reliable where it is most used is worse than one that is honestly scoped.

### No identity: support region edits only, and drop the enumerated form entirely (rejected)

- **Pros:** Removes the entire problem, along with fingerprints and positional restrictions, Keeps one edit form, so the model stays uniform and simple
- **Cons:** Cannot express the corrections that motivated the escape hatch — twelve strays among neighbours, Baking still needs to say which points a consolidated override applies to
- **Rejected because:** It would leave a real workflow unserved: isolating a handful of stray returns is a region only in the degenerate sense of enumerating them. Consolidation independently needs to name points, so removing identity does not remove the requirement — it only removes the honest specification of it.
